bibl.title: Equivalent inter- and intramodality long-term priming: Evidence for a common lexicon for words seen and words heard

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: null-result
span.quote: In sum, contrary to the standard observation, Experiment 1 showed an equivalence of inter- and intramodal priming.

span.label: cross-modal long-term word priming
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In five experiments, we employed manipulations aimed to minimize study–test asymmetries between the two priming conditions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Mixing study modalities within subjects pulls attention toward modality-specific processing and away from word phonology, so at test the stems whose modality matches the prime are the ones completed - manufacturing the apparent intramodal advantage.
span.quote: If the mixing of visual and auditory presentations draws attention to aspects of modality processing per se and away from word processing, then at test, those critical word stems sharing modality processing with the primes are more likely to be completed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Study-to-test carryover runs simultaneously along two dimensions - modality-independent lexical access, which yields the priming, and modality-dependent sensory analysis, which yields the overall performance difference between seeing and hearing.
span.quote: It is tempting to assume that this dichotomy reflects two different but co-occurring processes in implicit memory tasks: modality-independent lexical access and modality-dependent sensory analysis (see the General Discussion section).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Priming transfers through activation of a word's phonology, a code common to the word seen and the word heard, so its magnitude is unaffected by which sense delivered the prime.
span.quote: Its invariance over AV and VV rules out the distinct sensory qualities of seeing words and hearing words and points to the activation of phonology as the dimension of transfer.

span.label: The paper says it cannot say precisely why its results diverge from the conventional finding.
span.quote: At the current juncture, the precise reason is unclear.

span.label: The between-subjects design alone does not explain the contradiction with prior work, since other between-subjects studies did not find equivalence.
span.quote: As central as it may be, the between-subjects design that marks the present series of experiments cannot provide a complete account of the contradictory findings.

span.label: The account offered for the within-subjects asymmetry found in Experiment 3 is described as tentative.
span.quote: The identified asymmetry and the account given of it are obviously tentative, but not unreasonable.

span.label: intramodality
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory

span.label: implicit memory
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory

span.label: amodal lexicon
span.quote: The results point to a single amodal lexicon and to modality-independent phonological processing as the basis of implicit word memory

span.label: common lexicon
span.quote: Morton was led to reject the common lexicon hypothesis on the basis of experiments involving long-term priming conditions typical of implicit memory studies

span.label: long-term priming
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory

span.label: **TWO HYPOTHESES BUILT ON AN EFFECT, AND THE EFFECT TURNS OUT TO BE THE DESIGN:** `Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) SEPARATE VISUAL AND AUDITORY LEXICONS and (2) MODALITY DEPENDENCE OF IMPLICIT MEMORY.` Five experiments matching study activities, controlling phonological consistency and moving modality between subjects find `EQUAL MAGNITUDES`. **Kirsner1986, merged earlier today, reports intermodal priming `to a lesser extent than by intramodal` and reasons from it** - the corpus now holds the record that builds on the asymmetry and the record that dissolves it, twenty-one years apart
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory

span.label: **AND THE CONTROL THAT MAKES IT AN ARTEFACT CLAIM RATHER THAN A FAILED REPLICATION:** `A WITHIN-SUBJECTS EXPERIMENT YIELDED THE CONVENTIONAL INTRAMODALITY ADVANTAGE.` **The old effect comes back when the old design is used.** That is the strongest form this argument can take: not `we did not find it` but `here is the feature of the design that produces it, and here it is switched back on`. Compare erb2019 (Q-814), where removing a confound removed one of two effects - same logic, opposite direction
span.quote: A within-subjects experiment yielded the conventional intramodality advantage. The results point to a single amodal lexicon

span.label: **AND THE CONCLUSION NAMES BOTH THE STORE AND THE ROUTE:** `The results point to a SINGLE AMODAL LEXICON and to MODALITY-INDEPENDENT PHONOLOGICAL PROCESSING as the basis of implicit word memory.` Not merely that the two lexicons are one, but that what reaches it is phonology either way - which is why the experiments controlled whether words were `phonologically consistent`. **A positive mechanism offered alongside the negative result**, and it is testable: inconsistent words should behave differently, which the paper then examines
span.quote: The results point to a single amodal lexicon and to modality-independent phonological processing as the basis of implicit word memory

span.label: **AND IT IS THE FOURTH RECORD TODAY WHERE THE INSTRUMENT IS PART OF THE PHENOMENON.** Finkbeiner2011: the prime-classification task's difficulty decides what counts as subliminal. erb2019: associative-priming overlap decides whether a congruency sequence effect is control. eckstein2007: which awareness test you use decides whether the prime was seen. Here: whether modality is manipulated within or between subjects decides whether the lexicons look separate. **Four paradigms, one shape, and not one of them is a critique paper** - all four are ordinary empirical papers that had to clear the ground first
span.quote: A within-subjects experiment yielded the conventional intramodality advantage. The results point to a single amodal lexicon

span.label: contradicts → Morton (1979), hypothesis of separate visual and auditory lexicons
span.quote: Importantly, for the primary goal of the present research, the three conclusions for Experiment 2 run counter to the experimental observations that had led Morton (1979) to the hypothesis of separate lexicons for words seen and words heard.

span.label: contradicts → Pilotti, Gallo, and Roediger (2000, Experiment 3)
span.quote: In an experiment with auditory stem completion, Pilotti, Gallo, and Roediger (2000, Experiment 3) manipulated visual and auditory study between subjects and found better performance for auditory study, contrary to the present Experiments 1 and 2.

span.label: replicates → Brown et al. (1991), on design-dependence of modality effects
span.quote: This apparent dependence of relative performance in the two conditions on experimental design is in agreement with the observations of Brown et al.

span.label: intramodality —contrasted-with→ implicit memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE CONTRAST THE FIELD DREW AND THIS PAPER REMOVES.** The quote states the inference the weaker intermodality effect licensed - separate lexicons, and modality-dependent implicit memory - and the paper's five experiments take it away. Weight 0.9 and the quote is the position being tested rather than the finding; the finding is `equal magnitudes` and is quoted whole in the first sense. **A reader taking this triple alone gets the hypothesis, not the result** - which is the failure I dropped an edge for on eckstein2007 an hour ago. It survives here because `contrasted-with` is true under both readings: the two were contrasted, and that is what the paper is about.
span.quote: Weaker inter- than intramodality long-term priming of words has promoted two hypotheses: (1) separate visual and auditory lexicons and (2) modality dependence of implicit memory

span.label: long-term priming —operationalised-as→ implicit memory
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **THE PARADIGM IS THE MEASURE, AND THAT IS WHY THE ARTEFACT MATTERED SO MUCH.** Implicit memory is not observed directly; it is read off long-term priming, and the quote says so in the historical voice - Morton rejected a single lexicon on the strength of `long-term priming conditions TYPICAL OF implicit memory studies`. **If the asymmetry in those conditions is an artefact of study-test design, the rejection was an artefact too**, which is exactly the paper's argument. Weight 0.9: the operationalisation is the field's, stated plainly, not this paper's own construction.
span.quote: Morton was led to reject the common lexicon hypothesis on the basis of experiments involving long-term priming conditions typical of implicit memory studies

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: In neither ANOVA were any other factors significant.

span.label: mean
span.quote: The mean proportion of primed completions was .38 in VV and .30 in AV, relative to the unprimed baseline of .15.

span.label: Across five experiments using stem completion, fragment completion and perceptual identification at test, priming from a different study modality was as large as priming from the same modality.
span.quote: Equal magnitudes of inter- and intramodality priming were found in experiments with visual and auditory stem completion at test, with visual fragment completion at test, and with visual and auditory perceptual identification at test.

span.label: The authors conclude that one amodal lexicon serves words seen and words heard, and that implicit word memory rests on modality-independent phonological processing.
span.quote: The results point to a single amodal lexicon and to modality-independent phonological processing as the basis of implicit word memory.

span.label: In Experiment 1, auditory-study/visual-test stem completion primed as much as visual-study/visual-test stem completion, contrary to the standard intramodal advantage.
span.quote: In sum, contrary to the standard observation, Experiment 1 showed an equivalence of inter- and intramodal priming.

span.label: Experiment 2 found auditory-to-visual and visual-to-auditory transfer equal to each other, and auditory-to-auditory transfer equal to visual-to-visual transfer.
span.quote: First, cross-modal transfer occurs to the same degree in AV and VA. Second, AA transfer and VV transfer are of the same magnitude.

span.label: Experiment 3, which mixed study modalities within subjects and delivered all instructions visually, restored the conventional superiority of visual-to-visual over auditory-to-visual transfer.
span.quote: The within-subjects design of Experiment 3 benefited transfer in the same-modality condition, relative to the cross-modality condition.

span.label: In fragment completion (Experiment 4) the size of the priming effect was the same after visual and auditory study, but the overall level of fragment completion, primed and unprimed alike, was higher after visual study.
span.quote: The magnitude of priming was independent of stimulus modality, whereas the overall magnitude of fragment completion was modality dependent.

span.label: Deep study (imagery) and shallow study (counting ascenders/descenders, repeating the spoken word) produced equal priming, which the authors read as equal lexical involvement in the two tasks.
span.quote: The failure to find an influence on long-term priming of level of processing at study suggests that the processing tasks were alike in lexical involvement

span.label: identical study (first methodological step)
span.quote: In the first step, identified as identical study, we sought to ensure that the orientation at study would be the same whether the words were experienced visually or aurally.

span.label: modal homogeneity (fourth methodological step)
span.quote: A fourth step, identified as modal homogeneity, entailed minimizing switches in emphasis between looking and listening during study.

span.label: incidental study
span.quote: Study is incidental in an experiment when conditions (typically instructions) orient attention to an information-processing goal different from that of remembering the presented materials.

span.label: indirect memory test
span.quote: A memory test is indirect in an experiment when conditions orient attention to a current activity involving (surreptitiously) the material at study, without drawing attention to the prior incidence of study.

span.label: gestural phonology (gesture and gestural constellation)
span.quote: The primitives of gestural phonology are gestures and constellations of gestures of the vocal tract, where a gesture is a characteristic movement pattern of vocal tract articulators and a gestural constellation is a small number of potentially overlapping gestures composing an utterance.

span.label: study modality (visual vs auditory)
span.quote: Activities at visual and auditory study were matched, words were phonologically consistent, and study modality was manipulated between subjects.

span.label: priming condition (primed vs nonprimed items)
span.quote: The priming condition was a within-subjects factor, whereas group and modality were between-subjects factors.

span.label: proportion of stems completed with the target word (transfer measure and baseline measure)
span.term: proportion of stems completed with the target word (transfer measure and baseline measure)
span.quote: For each participant in each group, stem completion of the 12 primed critical stems (designated “P” in Appendix B) yielded the participant’s transfer measure, and stem completion of the 12 unprimed critical stems (designated “C” in Appendix B) yielded the participant’s baseline measure of stem completion performance

span.label: depth of the orienting task at study (deep vs shallow)
span.term: depth of the orienting task at study (deep vs shallow)
span.quote: There were two contrasting forms of incidental study: deep and shallow.

span.label: spelling-sound consistency of the study words
span.term: spelling-sound consistency of the study words
span.quote: The application of the two constraints, that on the orthography and that on the phonetics, was essentially the constraint of spelling–sound consistency in both directions

span.label: ratio of unstudied to studied words at test
span.term: ratio of unstudied to studied words at test
span.quote: The high 5:1 ratio of unstudied to studied words at test was for the purpose of reducing test awareness

span.label: .45 / .18 — Experiment 1, visual study-visual test: proportion of stems completed for primed words versus unprimed words
span.quote: For VV, the proportion of primed completions was .45, and the proportion of nonprimed completions was .18.

span.label: .44 / .10 — Experiment 1, auditory study-visual test: proportion of stems completed for primed words versus unprimed words
span.quote: For AV, the proportion of primed completions was .44, and the proportion of nonprimed completion was .10.

span.label: .38 vs .30 (baseline .15) — Experiment 3 (within-subjects design): primed stem completion for visual-to-visual versus auditory-to-visual, against the unprimed baseline
span.quote: The mean proportion of primed completions was .38 in VV and .30 in AV, relative to the unprimed baseline of .15.

span.label: 6% — size of the auditory-to-auditory advantage over visual-to-auditory in Experiment 5, which was tested separately
span.quote: Given the commonplace finding of samemodality superiority, the 6% superiority of AA over VA was evaluated separately.

span.label: 3.2 of the 26 — average number of critical primed words a participant could recall in the post-test memory check of Experiment 5
span.quote: On average, the participants recalled 3.2 of the 26 critical words (the primes).

span.label: 5:1 — ratio of unstudied to studied words on the test list, set to keep participants unaware of the study-test link
span.quote: The high 5:1 ratio of unstudied to studied words at test was for the purpose of reducing test awareness

span.label: 85% — share of Experiment 5 participants who said there was a connection between the three tasks
span.quote: Approximately 85% of the participants answered affirmatively.

span.label: Forty — number of undergraduates in Experiment 1, ten per group
span.quote: Forty undergraduates at the University of Connecticut participated in the experiment in partial fulfillment of an introductory psychology course requirement.

span.label: 86 — size of the base word pool from which critical, study-filler and test-filler words were drawn
span.quote: A basic set of 86 concrete words was selected in a nonprimed stem completion experiment.
